notes.meaning: Abraham's servant repeats how quickly Rebekah offered to give him water and draw water for his ten camels. He shares this detail so her family can see her humble, hard-working character. It also shows them that she acted in the exact way God had shown him in his prayer.

The servant explains that he learned who her father was before giving her the gifts. Finding out she was Bethuel's daughter proved she was from Abraham's own family, just as Abraham had required. Only after knowing God had answered his prayer did he put the nose-ring on her face and bracelets on her wrists.

The servant tells the family how he bowed his head and praised the Lord right there at the well. He gives all credit to God for guiding him on the right road to his master's relatives. True thankfulness responds to God's guidance with prompt and humble worship.

The servant asks the family for an honest answer right away. If they agree to the marriage, they show true loyalty and kindness to Abraham, but if they refuse, he must look for a bride elsewhere. He deals honestly with them and expects a clear answer in return.

Laban and Bethuel quickly agree to the marriage because they see that God has clearly arranged it. They realize it would be wrong to oppose the Lord's plain direction. They tell the servant to take Rebekah as a wife for Isaac, just as God has decreed.

Upon hearing their consent, the servant drops to the ground in worship before God. Before doing anything else, he thanks the Lord for answering his prayers and giving him success. Every new blessing should lead us to thank God anew.

The servant brings out fine clothing and vessels of silver and gold to give to Rebekah as a marriage dowry. He also gives costly gifts to her brother and mother to show Abraham's wealth and generous spirit. These presents sealed the marriage agreement and showed honor to her family.

Having completed his business, the servant and his companions sit down to eat, drink, and rest for the night. Early the next morning, he asks to be sent back immediately to his master. A faithful worker does not loiter or put his own comfort ahead of his duty.

Rebekah's mother and brother ask if she can stay with them for about ten more days before leaving. Because they loved her and knew she was moving far away, it was hard to say goodbye so suddenly. Even joyful moments in life often bring a touch of natural sorrow.

The servant urges them not to hold him back, since the Lord had already made his trip a success. He knew Abraham would be eagerly waiting to hear the news. When God opens the way for our duty, we should carry it out without unnecessary delay.

The family calls Rebekah to ask if she is willing to leave immediately, and she answers, 'I will go.' Her quick answer shows her faith and confidence that this union was truly the will of God. Parents guide marriage choices, but the person marrying must also give their own willing consent.

Her family sends Rebekah off with her childhood nurse, who would provide familiar comfort and support among strangers. She leaves accompanied by the servant and his men for safe travel. The nurse was a trusted, lifelong helper who stayed by her side.

Her family pronounces a loving blessing over Rebekah as she departs. They pray that her children will become countless in number and will conquer the cities of their enemies. Unknown to them, this blessing echoed God's covenant promises to Abraham.

Rebekah and her maidservants climb onto the camels and set out behind Abraham's servant. Having servants of her own proves that her earlier work at the well was done out of humble kindness, not out of poverty. She willingly leaves her old home behind to step into God's plan.

Isaac is living in the dry southern desert region and has just come from the well called Beer-lahai-roi. That well was famous as the place where God had previously seen and answered Hagar in her distress. Living near this quiet place encouraged a life of faith and relying on God's watchcare.

Isaac walks out into the open field in the quiet of the evening to pray and think about God. While spending this peaceful time alone with the Lord, he looks up and sees the camels returning. God's blessings often meet us when we are quietly doing our duty and seeking Him in prayer.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest the rare Hebrew word here means to mourn or lament, indicating Isaac had walked out into the field specifically to grieve his recently deceased mother.

notes.meaning: When Rebekah spots Isaac walking in the field, she quickly steps down from her camel. In ancient Eastern culture, it was considered rude to remain seated on an animal while an honored person approached on foot. Her quick descent was a sign of deep respect for her future husband.

After the servant tells her the approaching man is his master Isaac, Rebekah covers her face with a veil. Wearing a veil was the customary sign of a bride's modesty, purity, and respect toward her husband. She conducts herself with dignity and grace as they meet.

The faithful servant reports everything that happened during his journey to Isaac. He tells of his prayer at the well, Rebekah's generous actions, and her family's clear agreement. Hearing this full account assures Isaac that God Himself had chosen this bride for him.

Isaac brings Rebekah into his late mother Sarah's tent, takes her as his wife, and truly loves her. Sarah had died about three years earlier, and Isaac's deep sorrow is finally healed through the joy of his new marriage. A godly marriage is built on mutual commitment, genuine affection, and God's comforting care.

differ.view: Many see Isaac and Rebekah as a prophetic picture of Jesus and the Church, where the Father sends the Spirit like the servant to call and lavish gifts upon a bride for His Son.
